The January 30, 2019 FOMC statement pivots to “patience,” maintaining confidence in a solid expansion and strong labor markets with inflation near 2%, and keeps the federal funds rate at 2.25–2.50% (IOER at 2.40%) within the post-2008 floor system. Incorporating the SLOOS, however, tilts the overall read more cautious than the headline macro tone suggests:

- Banks reported tighter standards for C&I loans and construction/land development loans, alongside wider loan rate spreads and weaker demand for business credit; they also expected tighter standards for C&I and CRE and weaker business loan demand through 2019.
- On household credit, standards were largely unchanged for some mortgage categories (e.g., GSE-eligible, HELOCs), but banks reported weaker demand for residential real estate loans and HELOCs, some tightening on consumer loans, and expectations of deteriorating performance for nonprime consumer credit.
- These credit supply and demand headwinds, coupled with lower market-based inflation compensation and global risks, validate the Committee’s patient, risk-management stance and help explain moderated business fixed investment.

Net tone: cautiously dovish and supportive of continued expansion, but tempered by softening credit conditions signaled by SLOOS. Adjusting for SLOOS, the sentiment is slightly less positive than before.
